prompt.context: Our client is the Chief Technology Officer (CTO) at a Fortune 100 retailer (Store A Co.) located in the United States. Store A Co. has made an offer to acquire its largest competitor (Store B Inc.) and FTC approval for the merger is expected in approximately 3 months. Our team is helping with synergy estimation and integration planning for the IT division. Store A Co. currently uses X-Mail as their vendor for corporate email and productivity software while Store B Inc. uses Y-Mail.
prompt.question: The CTO has asked us to help her select the go-forward vendor for email/productivity software for the combined company and provide her with the information she needs to justify the selection to the CEO and to the Board. How would you approach this problem?

clarifying_info.a: Productivity software includes word processing, spreadsheet, and slide making applications.

clarifying_info.q: What type of email/productivity solution do they use?
clarifying_info.a: Both companies use a cloud-based solution analogous to Gmail and Google Docs or Microsoft Office 365 tools.

clarifying_info.q: Can the company pick a third-party vendor instead of X-Mail or Y-Mail?
clarifying_info.a: Theoretically yes, if there is a compelling case to do so, but there is additional risk in converting to a third solution.

clarifying_info.q: Do all employees need email/productivity access?
clarifying_info.a: No. All corporate employees require access. At the store level, only managers require access.

clarifying_info.q: Are there any additional costs beyond the monthly per-user fee?
clarifying_info.a: Yes. Migration and training cost $100 per person migrated, regardless of which solution is chosen.

clarifying_info.q: How much storage do users need?
clarifying_info.a: Users today need 3GB of storage; anything less would be very difficult to operate with.

clarifying_info.q: What does limited offline access mean for Y-Mail?
clarifying_info.a: Limited offline access means a user can only see their last 100 emails on their computer if they don't have an internet connection.

clarifying_info.q: What does limited calendar functionality mean for Y-Mail?
clarifying_info.a: Limited calendar functionality means a user can see their calendar on their phone but needs to use the computer to add events to it.

framework: Costs and synergy potential: How much does each solution cost per user? How many total users will need the solution? Are there one-time costs such as migration, training, or contract-breaking fees? What are the baseline costs pre-merger and what synergies does each option generate?
Qualitative assessment: What features does the combined company need? What features does each solution offer? Which solution is preferred by employees?
Risks and implementation: How many users would have to switch from their current solution? How long will implementation take? What are the risks of each option?

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, how many users will need the new solution, and how many users would undergo a change under each option?
questions.guidance: Candidate must recognize only corporate employees and store managers need access. Total users = 3000 corporate + (3 managers x 2000 stores) = 9000. Users changing under X-Mail (former Store B employees) = 1100 corporate + (3 x 1050 stores) = 4250. Users changing under Y-Mail (former Store A employees) = 1900 corporate + (3 x 950 stores) = 4750. Z-Mail would require all 9000 to change.

math.setup: Total users = corporate HQ employees + (managers per store x total stores). Users changing = legacy employees from the company not on that vendor.
steps: Users changing to X-Mail (legacy Store B) = 1100 corporate + 3 x 1050 stores = 1100 + 3150 = 4250
Users changing to Y-Mail (legacy Store A) = 1900 corporate + 3 x 950 stores = 1900 + 2850 = 4750
Users changing to Z-Mail = all 9000 (neither company uses Z-Mail)
math.answer: 9000 total users; 4250 change under X-Mail; 4750 change under Y-Mail; 9000 change under Z-Mail

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, what is the annual cost of each solution for the combined company, and what are the one-time migration costs?
questions.guidance: With 9000 users (6001-15000 tier): X-Mail $5/user/month, Y-Mail $4/user/month, Z-Mail $2/user/month. Annual costs: X-Mail $540K, Y-Mail $432K, Z-Mail $216K. Migration cost is $100 per person migrated: X-Mail $425K, Y-Mail $475K, Z-Mail $900K. Advanced: also calculate pre-merger baseline (Store A 5000 users on X-Mail at $6/month x 12 = $360K; Store B 5500 users on Y-Mail at $5/month x 12 = $330K; total baseline $690K). Synergy vs X-Mail = $690K - $540K = $150K; vs Y-Mail = $690K - $432K = $258K.

math.setup: 9000 users falls in the 6001-15000 tier. Annual cost = users x monthly rate x 12. Migration cost = users changing x $100.
steps: [Advanced] Store A pre-merger: 5000 users x $6 x 12 = $360,000
[Advanced] Store B pre-merger: 5500 users x $5 x 12 = $330,000
math.answer: Annual: X-Mail $540K, Y-Mail $432K, Z-Mail $216K. One-time migration: X-Mail $425K, Y-Mail $475K, Z-Mail $900K. Synergies vs baseline: X-Mail $150K, Y-Mail $258K.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 3, what do you conclude about the qualitative features of each solution?
questions.guidance: Z-Mail has only 1GB storage per user, which is below the 3GB minimum requirement — it should be eliminated. X-Mail has full features across all dimensions. Y-Mail has limited offline access and limited calendar functionality. Candidates should weigh whether these limitations are acceptable given Y-Mail's cost advantage. The candidate must justify any exclusion of Y-Mail based on the business impact of the limited features; they should not eliminate Y-Mail without reasoning.

recommendation: Recommend X-Mail or Y-Mail (either is defensible with proper justification). Sample recommendation for X-Mail: Select X-Mail as the go-forward email and productivity platform. It is a feature-rich solution with full offline access and full calendar functionality that minimizes transition risk. Annual run-rate cost is $540K with a one-time migration cost of $425K, and delivers $150K in annual synergies vs. the pre-merger baseline.

Sample recommendation for Y-Mail: Select Y-Mail for a lower annual run-rate of $432K delivering $258K in annual synergies, accepting limited offline access and calendar functionality as manageable trade-offs for the cost savings.
risks: X-Mail risk: Higher annual run-rate cost ($540K vs $432K for Y-Mail) and lower synergy value ($150K vs $258K).

Y-Mail risk: More users undergo a change (4750 vs 4250 for X-Mail), including more corporate HQ employees who likely use email more intensively, increasing implementation and disruption risk. Limited offline access and limited calendar functionality may impact productivity.

Z-Mail risk: Does not meet the 3GB storage minimum requirement; requires all 9000 users to migrate at a one-time cost of $900K; no productivity suite, calendar, directory, or security — should be eliminated.
Third-party vendor risk: Switching to an entirely new vendor introduces the highest implementation risk and unknown feature/cost profile.
For a Fortune 100 retailer, these annual cost differences are relatively small; the decision may ultimately come down to risk tolerance and change management capacity.
next_steps: Validate user counts with HR and IT teams at both companies before finalizing the budget.
Assess employee satisfaction and preference through a brief survey, particularly among heavy corporate users.
Develop a detailed migration and training plan, including timeline and phased rollout by employee group.
Quantify productivity loss during transition period as part of the total cost of implementation.
Present the analysis — annual cost, one-time migration cost, synergy value, and feature trade-offs — to the CEO and Board as a formal recommendation package.
